title: EUR 140,000 cover treated as a different kind of payment
explain:
A EUR 140,000 cover payment arrived.
The team treated it as a different kind of movement from a serial payment.
They built separate handling for it, and the cover leg stalled while they worked out rules that already existed.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT202 COV arrives
→ Team treats it as a new kind of payment
→ Separate handling built from scratch
→ Cover leg stalls

The assumption was:
"A cover is a different kind of movement."
The cover is the same serial mechanism carrying the funds leg.

Why?

Looked at on its own, an MT202 COV is a serial payment: the sender instructs the receiver to debit the sender's account and credit the next bank in the chain. Each bank in the cover chain debits the previous bank's account and instructs the next bank, until the funds reach the beneficiary bank.

The cover is the same serial mechanism carrying the funds leg of a customer payment.

What proves we handled the cover leg with the rules we already have?

BA Takeaway

Handle an MT202 COV as a serial payment: debit the sender's account, credit the next bank, instruct the next bank in the chain. Apply the serial rules you already have, instead of inventing new ones.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Sender debited
→ Next bank credited
→ Next bank instructed
→ Funds reach the beneficiary bank

The real requirement isn't "What kind of payment is a cover?"

It's "What evidence proves we handled the cover leg with the rules we already have?"

Have you ever built new handling for a cover that the serial rules already covered?
takeaway: The cover is the same serial mechanism carrying the funds leg of a customer payment.

title: EUR 1,200 in charges taken from a EUR 200,000 cover
explain:
A EUR 200,000 cover payment arrived EUR 1,200 short.
An intermediary had taken its charges straight from the cover.
An MT191 then arrived, claiming the same charges again.

Here's how that happens:

→ Cover arrives EUR 1,200 short
→ Intermediary took charges from the cover
→ MT191 arrives claiming the same charges
→ Customer charged twice for one leg

The assumption was:
"Charges come out of the funds in transit."
Charges must not be deducted from a cover payment.

Why?

When one bank owes another bank charges or interest on a payment, the claim travels in an MT191, a request for payment of charges, and the advice travels in an MT190. These messages exist because charges must not be deducted from a cover payment, so an intermediary that is owed money asks for it separately instead of taking it from the funds.

An MT191 in a chain is the charges leg, not the payment itself.

What proves the charges were claimed separately, not taken from the cover?

BA Takeaway

Claim charges with an MT191 and advise them with an MT190. Never take them from the cover, and check that a charge claimed by MT191 was not also deducted from the funds.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cover amount in full
→ MT191 claim
→ MT190 advice
→ No double charge

The real requirement isn't "Were the charges taken from the cover?"

It's "What evidence proves the charges were claimed separately, not taken from the cover?"

Have you ever found the same charges claimed twice, once from the cover and once by MT191?
takeaway: An MT191 in a chain is the charges leg, not the payment itself.

title: USD 60,000 sent in dollars, credited short after a double conversion
explain:
USD 60,000 was sent to a United States dollar account.
The beneficiary was credited short.
An intermediary had converted the payment twice on the way, and no one had asked for a conversion.

Here's how that happens:

→ Sender sends USD 60,000
→ Intermediary converts the payment
→ Second intermediary converts it again
→ Beneficiary credited short in dollars

The assumption was:
"Intermediaries can convert as they pass the payment on."
No intermediary may change the currency.

Why?

The sender decides the currency of a transaction, and no intermediary may change it on the way. If the beneficiary's account is in a different currency, the conversion happens as a separate foreign exchange step, and the beneficiary is credited in the currency of the account.

A payment sent in dollars to a dollar account that arrives short after a double conversion has gone wrong.

What proves no intermediary changed the currency on the way?

BA Takeaway

Pass the currency unchanged through every intermediary. Convert only as a separate foreign exchange step when the beneficiary's account is in another currency, and challenge any bank in the chain when a same-currency payment arrives short.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Currency sent
→ Currency at each intermediary
→ Separate FX step if needed
→ Currency credited

The real requirement isn't "Was the currency changed on the way?"

It's "What evidence proves no intermediary changed the currency on the way?"

Have you ever had to challenge a bank over a same-currency payment that arrived short?
takeaway: A payment sent in dollars to a dollar account that arrives short after a double conversion has gone wrong.

title: USD 100,000, and the beneficiary received less than the sender instructed
explain:
A sender instructed USD 100,000 with field 71A as BEN.
The beneficiary was credited as if the instruction had been SHA.
The beneficiary received less than the sender had instructed, and the bank copy showed a different code from the sender's instruction.

Here's how that happens:

→ Sender instructs 71A BEN
→ Each bank deducts its charge
→ Beneficiary bears every charge
→ Bank copy shows SHA, beneficiary credited differently

The assumption was:
"The bank copy is just a copy."
A bank copy that shows SHA where the sender instructed BEN is a discrepancy worth querying.

Why?

When field 71A carries BEN, every charge in the chain is borne by the beneficiary, and each bank deducts its charge from the amount as the payment passes through. The sender does not prepay the downstream charges, because the beneficiary is the one who pays them.

A bank copy that shows SHA where the sender instructed BEN is a discrepancy worth querying.

What proves the charge code on the bank copy matches the sender's instruction?

BA Takeaway

Check field 71A on the bank copy against the sender's instruction before the payment goes out. Query any copy that shows SHA where BEN was instructed, because the two codes give the beneficiary a different amount.

Keep these controls separate:

→ 71A on the instruction
→ 71A on the bank copy
→ Charges deducted
→ Beneficiary credit

The real requirement isn't "Does the code on the copy matter?"

It's "What evidence proves the charge code on the bank copy matches the sender's instruction?"

Have you ever caught a charge code changed between the instruction and the bank copy?
takeaway: A bank copy that shows SHA where the sender instructed BEN is a discrepancy worth querying.

title: EUR 55,000 MT103 with a BIC stuffed into field 57B
explain:
A EUR 55,000 MT103 arrived with field 57B carrying a BIC.
The receiving system could not route it straight through.
The payment stopped for manual handling, because a BIC must never be passed in option B.

Here's how that happens:

→ Field 57B carries a BIC
→ Receiving system cannot straight-through process it
→ Payment stops for manual handling
→ Correct option, A, never used

The assumption was:
"The BIC is in the field, so the bank is identified."
Option B carries a party identifier, generally an account number, with the location of the account.

Why?

Field 57 offers four options, and option A, with a BIC, is the one that allows straight-through processing. Option D needs no routing code at all and can simply carry the bank's name and address, while the /C/ or /D/ code before an account number is part of the standard but almost never used in practice.

Option A is the default whenever a BIC is available.

What proves the right option was used for the identifier we had?

BA Takeaway

Use option A whenever a BIC is available. Use option B only for a party identifier such as an account number with its location, and option D for a name and address with no routing code.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Identifier available
→ Option chosen
→ Straight-through processing achieved

The real requirement isn't "Is the BIC in the message?"

It's "What evidence proves the right option was used for the identifier we had?"

Have you ever seen an STP payment stop because a BIC was put in the wrong option?
takeaway: Option A is the default whenever a BIC is available.

title: USD 80,000 to a US bank, and the clearing account was a guess
explain:
USD 80,000 was sent to a United States bank.
Field 57A carried only the BIC.
The receiving bank had several clearing accounts, and the operations team had to guess which one the payment was for.

Here's how that happens:

→ Field 57A carries the BIC only
→ Receiving bank holds several clearing accounts
→ No CHIPS UID to pin down the account
→ Payment held while the account is confirmed

The assumption was:
"The BIC alone is always enough."
Using the BIC alone is valid, but the UID removes any doubt.

Why?

In option A of field 57, the line before the BIC is the party identifier, and for a United States payment that identifier can be the beneficiary bank's CHIPS UID. The CHIPS UID identifies the bank in the United States clearing system, while the BIC identifies it on SWIFT, so the two sit together in the same field.

The BIC alone is valid, but the UID removes any doubt about which clearing account should be used.

What proves the payment will land in the right clearing account?

BA Takeaway

Put the CHIPS UID on the party identifier line before the BIC in field 57A for United States payments. The BIC names the bank on SWIFT, the UID names its clearing account, and together they leave no doubt.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Party identifier line
→ CHIPS UID
→ BIC
→ Clearing account pinned down

The real requirement isn't "Is the BIC enough?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment will land in the right clearing account?"

Have you ever had to guess which clearing account a payment was for?
takeaway: The BIC alone is valid, but the UID removes any doubt about which clearing account should be used.

title: EUR 110,000 debited from the wrong nostro account
explain:
A bank held three euro accounts with the same correspondent.
EUR 110,000 was debited from the wrong one.
Liquidity planning for the week broke, because field 53B had never named the account to debit.

Here's how that happens:

→ Bank holds several accounts with one correspondent
→ Field 53 left vague
→ Wrong nostro account debited
→ Liquidity plan breaks

The assumption was:
"Field 53 always means the nostro account."
Field 53 does not always contain the sender's nostro account.

Why?

A bank can hold more than one account with the same correspondent in the same currency, and field 53B exists to say exactly which account must be debited. Using option B tells the receiver that the sender has many accounts with it and wants a specific one used to settle the transaction.

Field 53B exists to say exactly which account must be debited.

What proves the right account was debited?

BA Takeaway

Use field 53B to name the exact account to debit whenever the sender holds more than one account with the receiver. Remember that field 53 itself is optional in an MT103, and its three options can carry different information.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Accounts held with the correspondent
→ Field 53B account named
→ Account debited
→ Liquidity plan intact

The real requirement isn't "Which account was debited?"

It's "What evidence proves the right account was debited?"

Have you ever found a payment debited from the wrong nostro account?
takeaway: Field 53B exists to say exactly which account must be debited.

title: EUR 35,000 remittance reference that broke the 16-character limit
explain:
A EUR 35,000 payment carried a remittance reference in field 70.
The reference after /RFB/ ran past 16 characters.
The beneficiary's system could not match it, and the payment sat unreconciled.

Here's how that happens:

→ Field 70 carries several references
→ /RFB/ reference runs past 16 characters
→ Beneficiary system cannot match it
→ Payment sits unreconciled

The assumption was:
"A longer reference is a clearer reference."
The reference that follows /RFB/ is limited to 16 characters.

Why?

Field 70 carries remittance information, and several references can be given if they are separated by a double slash, but one code such as /RFB/ or /INV/ cannot serve two references of the same kind. A longer description must continue on the following lines of the field instead of stretching the reference.

A field 70 that repeats a code or overruns the limit is not a valid instruction.

What proves field 70 follows the limits?

BA Takeaway

Keep the reference after /RFB/ within 16 characters. Use one code per reference kind, separate references with a double slash, and put longer text on the following lines, not inside the reference.

Keep these controls separate:

→ References separated by double slash
→ One code per reference kind
→ /RFB/ within 16 characters
→ Longer text on following lines

The real requirement isn't "Is the reference clear enough?"

It's "What evidence proves field 70 follows the limits?"

Have you ever seen a payment sit unreconciled over a reference that was too long?
takeaway: A field 70 that repeats a code or overruns the limit is not a valid instruction.

title: EUR 48,000 credited to the named beneficiary when it belonged further on
explain:
EUR 48,000 was sent to a named beneficiary.
The funds were meant for an account beyond that beneficiary.
The beneficiary bank credited the named beneficiary directly, because no instruction told it to look further.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 names the beneficiary in field 59
→ Funds meant for a further account
→ No /FFC/ instruction in field 72
→ Beneficiary credited directly, onward account never paid

The assumption was:
"The beneficiary bank will know where the funds really belong."
Without the code, the bank has no instruction to look beyond the beneficiary named in field 59.

Why?

When the funds must be credited to an account other than the beneficiary's own account, the instruction travels as /FFC/, for further credit, in field 72, sender to receiver information. The beneficiary bank reads the code and passes the funds on to the account named after it, instead of crediting the beneficiary directly.

Without the code, the bank has no instruction to look beyond the beneficiary named in field 59.

What proves the funds were meant to go further than the named beneficiary?

BA Takeaway

Put /FFC/ in field 72 with the onward account named after it, whenever the funds belong beyond the beneficiary. Check field 72 before sending, because the beneficiary bank will only do what the instruction says.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Beneficiary in field 59
→ /FFC/ in field 72
→ Onward account named
→ Funds passed onward

The real requirement isn't "Is the beneficiary the final account?"

It's "What evidence proves the funds were meant to go further than the named beneficiary?"

Have you ever seen funds stop at the named beneficiary when they belonged further on?
takeaway: Without the code, the bank has no instruction to look beyond the beneficiary named in field 59.

title: EUR 160,000 late, and the MT103 copy proved nothing
explain:
EUR 160,000 was late by four days.
The customer produced a copy of the MT103 as proof the money had moved.
The copy proved nothing, and the bank could not trace the payment from it.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment late by four days
→ Customer shows a copy of the MT103
→ Copy proves nothing about whether the money moved
→ Bank cannot trace the payment from the copy

The assumption was:
"An MT103 copy proves the money moved."
A copy of an MT103 on its own proves nothing about whether the money moved.

Why?

The unique end-to-end transaction reference, the UETR, is carried in field 121 of block 3 of the message header, not in the body of the MT103. When a payment is late or a bank cannot trace it, the UETR is the reference to give the bank, because every bank in the chain can use it to follow the payment across the network.

A copy of an MT103 on its own proves nothing about whether the money moved.

What proves this payment moved, and where it is now?

BA Takeaway

Trace with the UETR from field 121 of block 3, together with the sending bank's records. Give the bank the UETR, not a copy of the MT103, and let every bank in the chain follow the same reference.

Keep these controls separate:

→ UETR in field 121 of block 3
→ Sending bank records
→ Every bank in the chain traces the same reference

The real requirement isn't "Do we have the MT103 copy?"

It's "What evidence proves this payment moved, and where it is now?"

Have you ever tried to trace a payment with only an MT103 copy?
takeaway: A copy of an MT103 on its own proves nothing about whether the money moved.

title: EUR 22,000 ordering name rejected for spilling onto a second line
explain:
An ordering customer had a long company name.
It ran over two lines in field 50K.
The receiving bank rejected the MT103, saying a name must fit on one line.

Here's how that happens:

→ Ordering customer name spans two lines in field 50K
→ Receiving bank rejects the message
→ Payment for EUR 22,000 stops
→ Sender told the name must fit on one line

The assumption was:
"A name must fit on the first line."
The standard does not restrict the name to the first line.

Why?

Option K of field 50a allows the ordering customer's name and address in up to four lines of 35 characters each. The name does not have to fit on the first line: it can sit on one line with the address on the rest, or run over two or three lines with the address on what remains.

The standard does not restrict the name to the first line, so a name split across lines is valid.

What proves a name split across lines is valid in field 50K?

BA Takeaway

Use the four lines of 35 characters as the standard allows. Put the name on one line with the address on the rest, or let the name run over two or three lines, and challenge any rejection that claims a name must fit on one line.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Four lines of 35 characters
→ Name on one line, address on the rest
→ Name over two or three lines valid

The real requirement isn't "Does the name fit on one line?"

It's "What evidence proves a name split across lines is valid in field 50K?"

Have you ever seen a payment rejected because a name spilled onto a second line?

title: EUR 85,000 MT101, and the two references pointed at two different owners
explain:
An MT101 for EUR 85,000 carried two references.
Field 20 and field 21R showed different values.
The operations team treated them as the same reference, and the reconciliation broke.

Here's how that happens:

→ Field 20 assigned by the sending bank
→ Field 21R assigned by the ordering customer
→ Team treats them as one reference
→ Reconciliation breaks

The assumption was:
"Two references on one message are the same reference."
They belong to different parties.

Why?

Field 20 is the sender's reference, assigned by the bank that sends the MT101 to identify the payment. Field 21R is the ordering customer's reference, assigned by the customer who ordered the payment, and it stays the same across every message sent for one order. The two references can coincide when the sender is also the ordering customer, but they belong to different parties, and field 21R is optional while field 20 is mandatory.

Field 20 belongs to the sender. Field 21R belongs to the ordering customer.

What proves we matched this payment on the right reference?

BA Takeaway

Match on field 20 for the sender's reference and on field 21R for the ordering customer's reference, which stays the same across every message for one order. Never merge the two.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 20 mandatory
→ Field 21R optional
→ Field 21R stable across messages
→ Match on the right reference

The real requirement isn't "Are the two references the same?"

It's "What evidence proves we matched this payment on the right reference?"

Have you ever seen two references on one message treated as one?
takeaway: Field 20 belongs to the sender. Field 21R belongs to the ordering customer.

title: EUR 120,000 paid by a parent, and the beneficiary thanked the wrong company
explain:
A parent company paid EUR 120,000 on behalf of a subsidiary.
The beneficiary thanked the parent for a payment the subsidiary had really made.
The subsidiary's own records showed nothing, because the beneficiary had been told the payment was from the subsidiary, and no one had read the field that said so.

Here's how that happens:

→ Parent sends the MT101
→ Subsidiary named in the Instructing Party field
→ Beneficiary sees the parent as the sender
→ Beneficiary thanks the wrong company

The assumption was:
"The sender is the party the payment is from."
The beneficiary is told the payment is from the subsidiary through the Instructing Party field.

Why?

When a parent company sends an MT101 to pay on behalf of a subsidiary, the parent company stands as the sender, not the subsidiary. The beneficiary is told the payment is from the subsidiary through the Instructing Party field, which names the subsidiary even though the parent sent the instruction.

The beneficiary sees the parent as the sender and the subsidiary as the party the payment is really from.

What proves the beneficiary knows which company this payment is really from?

BA Takeaway

Name the subsidiary in the Instructing Party field on every MT101 sent for it. Read that field before telling a beneficiary who paid them, and record the payment under the subsidiary, not the sender.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Sender is the parent
→ Instructing Party names the subsidiary
→ Beneficiary told the real source
→ Recorded under the subsidiary

The real requirement isn't "Who paid this?"

It's "What evidence proves the beneficiary knows which company this payment is really from?"

Have you ever seen a beneficiary thank the wrong company for a payment?
takeaway: The beneficiary sees the parent as the sender and the subsidiary as the party the payment is really from.

title: One MT101 for EUR 500,000 across six banks, or six MT101s
explain:
A large corporate held accounts at six banks.
It had to pay EUR 500,000 across them.
The team prepared six separate MT101s, one per bank, and spent a day on work one message could have done.

Here's how that happens:

→ Corporate holds accounts at many banks
→ Six MT101s prepared, one per bank
→ Day spent on six messages
→ One MT101 to a concentrating bank would have done it

The assumption was:
"Each bank needs its own MT101 from us."
One MT101 to a concentrating bank is enough.

Why?

A large corporate with accounts at many banks can send a single MT101 to one concentrating bank, and that bank forwards the instruction to each bank that holds an account to be debited. The alternative is for the corporate to prepare a separate MT101 for every bank, which is slower and harder to manage.

The forwarding service is a genuine value-added service, and the concentrating bank charges for it.

What proves one MT101 reached every bank that had to be debited?

BA Takeaway

Send one MT101 to the concentrating bank and let it forward the instruction to each bank holding an account to be debited. Agree the forwarding charge upfront, and confirm every leg was forwarded.

Keep these controls separate:

→ One MT101 sent
→ Concentrating bank forwards
→ Every bank debited
→ Forwarding charge agreed

The real requirement isn't "Do we need one MT101 per bank?"

It's "What evidence proves one MT101 reached every bank that had to be debited?"

Have you ever prepared six messages when one would have done?
takeaway: The forwarding service is a genuine value-added service, and the concentrating bank charges for it.

title: EUR 2 million payroll split across five MT101s, and one arrived late
explain:
A EUR 2 million payroll order was too big for one MT101.
It was split across five messages, numbered 1 of 5 to 5 of 5.
Message 4 arrived a day late, and the bank processed the rest without it.

Here's how that happens:

→ Order exceeds the 10,000 character limit
→ Order split across five MT101s
→ Messages numbered in field 28D
→ Message 4 arrives late, others processed alone

The assumption was:
"Each message in the chain can be processed as it arrives."
Banks hold a chained message until every message in the chain has arrived.

Why?

An MT101 message is limited to 10,000 characters, so an order with many transactions must be split across several MT101 messages, numbered in field 28D as 1 of 5, 2 of 5, and so on. Processing one element alone could pay the wrong amounts.

Banks hold a chained message until every message in the chain has arrived.

What proves every message in the chain arrived before any was processed?

BA Takeaway

Number every message in field 28D and hold the chain until all of them have arrived. Agree very large orders with the bank before sending, because banks set their own limits on how many transactions they will accept in one order.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 28D numbering
→ All messages arrived
→ Chain held until complete
→ Large order agreed with the bank

The real requirement isn't "Can we process the messages that arrived?"

It's "What evidence proves every message in the chain arrived before any was processed?"

Have you ever seen part of a chained order processed without the rest?
takeaway: Banks hold a chained message until every message in the chain has arrived.

title: EUR 15,000 moved inside one bank, and the team still sent an MT103
explain:
EUR 15,000 moved between two accounts at the same bank.
The team sent an MT101, then an MT103 as well.
The MT103 went nowhere, because the payment never left the bank.

Here's how that happens:

→ Same bank holds both accounts
→ Payment never leaves the bank
→ Single MT101 sent
→ MT103 sent too, for a payment that needs no interbank message

The assumption was:
"Every payment needs an MT103."
An MT103 is only required when the beneficiary's bank is different from the debtor's bank.

Why?

If the same bank holds both the debtor's account and the beneficiary's account, the payment never leaves the bank, so no interbank message is needed. A single MT101 is enough: the bank debits the debtor's account and credits the beneficiary's account on its own books.

An MT103 is only required when the beneficiary's bank is different from the debtor's bank.

What proves this payment needed no interbank message?

BA Takeaway

Check whether both accounts sit at the same bank before choosing the message. Same bank means one MT101 and a book transfer. Different banks means an MT103.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Debtor bank
→ Beneficiary bank
→ Same bank or different
→ Message chosen

The real requirement isn't "Do we need an MT103 for this?"

It's "What evidence proves this payment needed no interbank message?"

Have you ever sent an interbank message for a payment that never left the bank?
takeaway: An MT103 is only required when the beneficiary's bank is different from the debtor's bank.

title: EUR 4 million statement, and the closing balance appeared twice
explain:
A EUR 4 million statement was split across several MT940 messages.
An intermediate message carried tag 62F, the final closing balance.
The client system treated the statement as finished and never generated the messages that followed.

Here's how that happens:

→ Statement split across several MT940s
→ Intermediate message carries tag 62F
→ Client system treats the statement as finished
→ Later messages never generated

The assumption was:
"Every message can carry a closing balance."
There is only one closing balance for the whole statement.

Why?

A statement split across several MT940 messages must use the intermediate closing balance, tag 62M, in every message except the last. Only the final message carries the final closing balance, tag 62F.

There is only one closing balance for the whole statement.

What proves the closing balance appears only on the final message?

BA Takeaway

Use tag 62M on every intermediate message and tag 62F only on the last. Check the tag on every message in the chain before sending, because one early 62F ends the statement for the receiver.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Tag 62M on intermediate messages
→ Tag 62F only on the final message
→ One closing balance
→ Receiver generates every message

The real requirement isn't "Can this message carry the closing balance?"

It's "What evidence proves the closing balance appears only on the final message?"

Have you ever seen a statement end early because of one wrong tag?
takeaway: There is only one closing balance for the whole statement.

title: EUR 4 million statement, and the intermediate balance dates did not match
explain:
A EUR 4 million statement arrived as several MT940s.
The intermediate balance dates did not match the last entry in each message.
The receiver questioned the statement, even though the balances themselves were right.

Here's how that happens:

→ Statement split across several MT940s
→ Tags 60M and 62M show the wrong dates
→ Balances correct, dates do not match the last entry
→ Receiver questions the statement

The assumption was:
"Only the balances matter, the dates do not."
The dates that truly matter are the opening, closing, closing available and forward available balances, and the intermediate dates should match the last entry.

Why?

When a statement is split across several MT940 messages, the intermediate opening balance tag 60M and the intermediate closing balance tag 62M should ideally show the date of the last entry in that message. In practice receivers care most that the balances themselves are correct.

Receivers care most that the balances themselves are correct.

What proves the intermediate dates match the last entry in each message?

BA Takeaway

Set tags 60M and 62M to the date of the last entry in each message. Fix the intermediate dates whenever they can be fixed easily, and always get the opening, closing, closing available and forward available balance dates right.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Tags 60M and 62M
→ Date of the last entry
→ Balances correct
→ Key balance dates right

The real requirement isn't "Do the intermediate dates matter?"

It's "What evidence proves the intermediate dates match the last entry in each message?"

Have you ever had a statement questioned over a balance date?
takeaway: Receivers care most that the balances themselves are correct.

title: A statement with 900 entries arrived as one MT940, and the rest never came
explain:
A statement with 900 entries was sent as a single MT940.
Only the first entries arrived.
The rest never came, because a single MT940 can carry only a limited number of entries.

Here's how that happens:

→ Statement has 900 entries
→ Single MT940 sent
→ Only the first entries arrive
→ Rest of the statement never comes

The assumption was:
"One statement, one message."
A statement with many entries is split across several MT940 messages, one after another.

Why?

Each message carries a statement number and a sequence number, and the sequence number rises with each new message, so the receiver can put the statement back together in order. The chain can run to a very large number of sequences, which is more than enough in practice.

The sequence number rises with each message, so the receiver can rebuild the order.

What proves the receiver got every part of the statement, in order?

BA Takeaway

Split long statements across several MT940s, one after another. Put the statement number and the rising sequence number on each message, and confirm the receiver rebuilt the full statement.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Entries per message
→ Statement number
→ Sequence number rising
→ Full statement rebuilt

The real requirement isn't "Was the whole statement sent?"

It's "What evidence proves the receiver got every part of the statement, in order?"

Have you ever received half a statement because it was sent as one message?
takeaway: The sequence number rises with each message, so the receiver can rebuild the order.

title: EUR 30,000 credit advice arrived in a format the receiver could not read
explain:
EUR 30,000 landed in a customer's account.
The credit advice arrived as a camt.054.
The receiver's system could only read MT900, so the customer was never told the money had arrived.

Here's how that happens:

→ Credit of EUR 30,000 applied
→ Advice sent as camt.054
→ Receiver can only read MT900
→ Customer never told the money arrived

The assumption was:
"Everyone reads the format we send."
No rule compels one format over the other, so the sender picks the form it will use.

Why?

When a bank tells its customer that a credit has landed, it may use a camt.054 in ISO 20022 or an MT900 in MT format, and both do the same job. The receiving side must therefore be ready to read either format when the advice arrives.

The receiving side must be ready to read either format when the advice arrives.

What proves the receiver can read whichever advice format arrives?

BA Takeaway

Build the receiving side to read both camt.054 and MT900. Agree the format with the sender where you can, but never assume the advice will arrive in the format you prefer.

Keep these controls separate:

→ camt.054 readable
→ MT900 readable
→ Format agreed where possible
→ Customer told on arrival

The real requirement isn't "Which format will the advice use?"

It's "What evidence proves the receiver can read whichever advice format arrives?"

Have you ever missed a credit because the advice arrived in a format you could not read?
takeaway: The receiving side must be ready to read either format when the advice arrives.

title: The MT950 arrived at noon. The team ignored it, and the day went wrong.
explain:
An MT950 for the account arrived at noon.
The team treated it as tomorrow's statement and ignored it.
By close of business the account was short and nobody knew why.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT950 received intraday
→ Team files it as the end of day statement
→ Intraday movements go unchecked
→ Shortfall found only at close of business

The requirement said:
"An MT950 is always the end of day statement."

Why?

An MT950 is normally the end of day statement, yet it can also be produced intraday alongside the MT940, when the account servicing bank and the account owner agree. That agreement sets what the receiver should expect during the day, and ignoring an intraday statement means ignoring live balances.

End of day is the default. Intraday is the agreement.

BA Takeaway

Check the agreement on every account before deciding what an MT950 means, and treat an intraday statement as live information.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Statement timing agreed
→ Intraday balances
→ End of day close

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves whether this MT950 is intraday or end of day?"

Have you ever missed a shortfall because a statement arrived earlier than expected?
takeaway: End of day is the default. Intraday is the agreement.

title: Twenty transactions, one closing balance, and EUR 4,000 that did not add up.
explain:
An MT950 shows twenty transactions and a closing balance.
The closing balance is EUR 4,000 out from the opening balance plus the entries.
The team trusts the balance and moves on.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT950 received with twenty field 61 entries
→ Field 62F closing balance read once
→ Opening balance plus field 61 entries checked
→ EUR 4,000 gap found in the arithmetic

The requirement said:
"The closing balance is always right."

Why?

Every transaction on an MT950 sits in its own repeating field 61, so twenty transactions mean twenty field 61 blocks. The closing balance in field 62F appears a single time, at the very end. That balance must agree with the opening balance plus all field 61 entries, and checking the arithmetic is the fastest completeness test.

Field 61 repeats. Field 62F must add up.

BA Takeaway

Recompute the closing balance from field 61 on every MT950 before trusting it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 61 entries
→ Field 62F closing balance
→ Opening balance

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this statement is complete?"

Have you caught a missing transaction just by adding up a statement?
takeaway: Field 61 repeats. Field 62F must add up.

title: EUR 75,000 moved. The statement shows it. Nobody knows why.
explain:
EUR 75,000 leaves the account.
The MT940 shows the movement in field 61.
The customer asks why it moved, and the team has no answer.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 75,000 debit on the MT940
→ Field 61 shows the date, amount and entry type
→ Field 86 checked for the narrative
→ No narrative found, customer query stalls

The requirement said:
"Field 61 is enough to reconcile a payment."

Why?

In an MT940, field 61 is the statement line, carrying the date, the amount and the entry type for each transaction. Field 86 sits beside that line and carries the information to the account owner, the narrative behind the movement. Field 61 alone shows that money moved. Field 86 shows why, and reconciliation needs both together.

Field 61 shows money moved. Field 86 shows why.

BA Takeaway

Never close a reconciliation on field 61 alone. Pair every line with its field 86 narrative.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 61 movement
→ Field 86 narrative
→ Reconciliation evidence

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves why this money moved, not just that it moved?"

Have you ever chased a payment the statement could show but never explain?

title: The treasurer thought EUR 2 million was available. It was not.
explain:
The treasurer reads the MT940 and sees EUR 2 million.
A payment of EUR 2 million is released against it.
The payment fails. The funds were never available that day.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT940 balances read at day end
→ EUR 2 million taken as available funds
→ Payment released against the wrong balance
→ Payment fails for lack of funds

The requirement said:
"The biggest balance on the statement is the money available."

Why?

Field 62M is the interim closing balance, struck when the statement was cut during the day. Field 64 is the closing available balance, the funds actually available at day end, while field 65 is the forward available balance, the funds expected on a future date. Confusing them overstates or understates liquidity, so each balance must be read for the question it answers.

62M, 64 and 65 answer different questions.

BA Takeaway

Name the question before reading a balance, and use only the field that answers it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ 62M interim balance
→ 64 closing available balance
→ 65 forward available balance

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves these funds are available today, not tomorrow?"

Have you ever seen a payment fail because the wrong balance was read?
takeaway: 62M, 64 and 65 answer different questions.

title: One MT940 never arrived. Nobody noticed for a week.
explain:
A week of statements arrives, and one MT940 is missing.
Every transaction in the week still reconciles.
The gap is found only when a customer disputes a payment from the missing day.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT940 statements arrive through the week
→ Field 28C sequence checked late
→ Gap found in the statement numbers
→ Missing day traced to a failed delivery

The requirement said:
"If the transactions reconcile, the statements are complete."

Why?

Field 28C carries the statement number and the sequence number, pinning down exactly which statement this is and where it sits in the run. A missing statement, or one arriving out of order, shows as a gap in the 28C sequence before any transaction is examined. That makes 28C the first completeness check on every MT940 received.

28C is the first completeness check.

BA Takeaway

Check the 28C sequence on arrival, before any transaction is examined.

Keep these controls separate:

→ 28C sequence
→ Statement delivery
→ Transaction reconciliation

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves no statement is missing from this run?"

Have you found a missing statement only after a customer complained?

title: EUR 250,000 went to the wrong correspondent. The instructions were published years ago.
explain:
A EUR 250,000 payment is sent to a correspondent named in the payment engine.
The correspondent no longer serves that currency.
The payment is rejected, and the team discovers the instructions were never updated.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment routed on stored settlement instructions
→ Correspondent named in the engine
→ Correspondent no longer serves the currency
→ Payment rejected downstream

The requirement said:
"Settlement instructions, once stored, stay correct."

Why?

Banks tell each other who their correspondents are through Standing Settlement Instructions, exchanged as SWIFT MT670 and MT671 messages, and receiving banks store them in their payment engines. The MT671 goes out to all SWIFT institutions, whether or not they hold a direct relationship with the sender. Where a bank has several correspondents in one currency it lists them all, leaving the sender to choose among them.

Published instructions go stale. Stored instructions go stale faster.

BA Takeaway

Treat settlement instructions as reference data with an owner and a refresh date, not as a one-time setup.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT670 and MT671 publication
→ Stored instructions
→ Correspondent choice

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this correspondent still serves this currency today?"

Have you seen a payment fail on instructions everyone assumed were current?
takeaway: Published instructions go stale. Stored instructions go stale faster.

title: EUR 600,000 of goods shipped. The documents were perfect. The bank paid nothing.
explain:
An exporter ships EUR 600,000 of goods under a documentary collection.
The documents are in order and the buyer pays.
The exporter then asks the collecting bank for the money, and the bank says it owes nothing.

Here is how that happens:

→ Documentary collection for EUR 600,000
→ Documents presented in order
→ Drawee pays what is due
→ Exporter claims payment from the collecting bank

The requirement said:
"If the documents are in order, the bank must pay."

Why?

In a documentary collection the collecting bank and the remitting bank act only as intermediaries between the drawer and the drawee. Unlike a documentary credit, the collecting bank owes the drawer no payment even when the documents are in order. It releases the documents to the drawee when the drawee pays what is due, and the payment undertaking found under a letter of credit simply does not exist here.

A collection intermediates. It never promises payment.

BA Takeaway

Say plainly in every collection requirement that the bank is an intermediary only, and name who actually pays.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Collecting bank role
→ Remitting bank role
→ Drawee payment

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves who owes the exporter this money?"

Have you seen a collection mistaken for a letter of credit?
takeaway: A collection intermediates. It never promises payment.

parts.label: Collecting bank intermediates

parts.label: Remitting bank intermediates
parts.note: It too acts only as an intermediary in the collection.

parts.note: The collecting bank owes no payment even if documents are in order.

parts.label: Documents released on payment

parts.note: The undertaking behind a letter of credit does not exist here.

title: A customer paid GBP 250 by card. The merchant was paid before the customer was.
explain:
A customer pays GBP 250 by card on Monday.
The merchant is paid at settlement on Tuesday.
The customer pays the issuer weeks later, after the statement arrives.

Here is how that happens:

→ Card used to pay GBP 250
→ Issuer sends the statement
→ Acquirer pays the merchant at settlement
→ Cardholder pays the issuer after the statement

The requirement said:
"The customer pays first, then the merchant gets paid."

Why?

Paying by card moves money in an order that surprises many people. First the card is used to pay, then the issuer sends the statement, then the merchant is paid by the acquirer at settlement, and finally the cardholder pays the issuer. The acquirer settles with the merchant every day across all transactions, while the cardholder's payment to the issuer comes only after the statement arrives.

The merchant is paid before the cardholder pays.

BA Takeaway

Explain the card order in every card requirement, so no one builds a flow that assumes the customer funds the merchant.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Card use
→ Acquirer settlement
→ Cardholder payment

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves who funded this transaction, and when?"

Did you know the merchant is paid before the cardholder pays?
takeaway: The merchant is paid before the cardholder pays.
